title: Why Teachers Agree to Things They Hate: Groupthink
author: Joel Kenyon
summary: Joel Kenyon, a UK science teacher and middle leader, argues that groupthink is one of the main reasons schools adopt initiatives that most staff privately reject. Using the Abilene paradox, pluralistic ignorance, and preference falsification, he shows how teachers nod along, click ten out of ten on feedback surveys, and praise CPD they found pointless because dissent risks being labelled uncooperative. He describes a five-step playbook: hype, bandwagon, pluralistic ignorance, distorted feedback, and institutional blindness, and uses question-level analysis and a 25-hour CPD course as examples from his own career. He then walks through how the pattern shows up in behaviour, curriculum, assessment, pedagogy, and SEND. His proposed remedy is a rotating, explicitly defined devil's advocate in every meeting, plus leaders who treat the absence of detractors as a warning sign.
points: Groupthink in schools is rarely top-down coercion; it is staff keeping their heads down because speaking up risks being branded anti-data, cynical, or not a team player.
Kenyon names a five-stage playbook (hype, bandwagon, pluralistic ignorance, distorted feedback, institutional blindness) that keeps flawed initiatives alive.
When compliance is rewarded and critique is not, new tasks stack up without anything being removed, which erodes the time-neutrality principle and burdens teachers.
CPD is a hotspot for preference falsification, since admitting a course was a waste means admitting the time spent on it was wasted too.

A clearly defined, rotating devil's advocate asking about workload, failure triggers, and what to remove can break the silence, and unanimous agreement in a meeting should itself be treated as a warning.
quotes: This is groupthink, specifically the Abilene paradox. Where a group of people take a course of action that very few actually wanted in the first place.

Groupthink in schools is not usually this overly authoritarian actively chosen path where the top demands X, Y and Z, but is a relatively large proportion of teachers keeping their heads down and nodding along when privately, they are weighing up the benefits and drawbacks of actually calling it out. Many just don’t say anything.

Pluralistic Ignorance: When the cracks start to show. Individual teachers assume they are the only ones questioning it. Rather than saying anything, they conform because “everyone else seems to love it.
Compliance is rewarded, critique is not. Therefore, you play the game, you jump the hoop, you do exactly what you are asked to do.

I hated it. I thought it was teaching me to suck eggs and it took 25 hours of my personal time. However, when it was brought in across the whole school, I had to say it was worth it because I would be admitting that I had wasted more than a days worth of time on something that was pointless.
In every meeting, especially leadership meetings, there should be one person who is the professional devil’s advocate that, ideally, changes in every meeting.

This one person being able to speak their mind freely enabled everyone the avenue to follow. By having the devil’s advocate present in every meeting, or even better, someone external reviewing the actions of the meeting, we break this continuous cycle doing what the most important person in the room wants rather than what may be better for the school as a whole.
Any discussion on something new in a school should have its detractors. I have been in far too many meetings where everyone just gets along with it despite disagreeing with it in private.
